newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi says making headway in balancing budget.
newsitem.headline: Saudi says making headway in balancing budget.

text.p: After over a decade of suffering budget deficits, Saudi Arabia has made good headway in its drive to balance state spending and revenue, Finance and National Economy Minister Ibrahim Abdel Aziz al-Asaf said.

"We have taken big steps towards the first aim which is to work to achieve a financial balance between revenue and expenditure," the official Saudi Press Agency (SPA) quoted Asaf as saying late on Wednesday.
"...The deficit in the government budget decreased in a big way from the last years and the effects of liberating Kuwait on the budget of the government are receding," he added.

Saudi Arabia on Monday announced its 1997 budget, projecting a deficit of 17 billion riyals ($4.5 billion) -- steady at the actual 1996 deficit, but below the 18.5 billion spending-revenue gap forecast for the year last January.
"The reasons for this decrease is due to two factors...work continued to squeeze and rationalise spending...revenue...went up more than projected last year, especially oil," he added.

Stronger oil prices -- which in 1996 shot up to the highest level since the 1990-91 Gulf War -- pushed the world's largest oil producer and exporter's 1996 earnings up to 177 billion riyals compared to a forecast 131.5 billion.
Asked how the deficit would be covered he said: "We will continue to work in the same direction of the last few years which is to limit borrowing to internal borrowing."
He said the king has said the country must avoid foreign borrowing and that any borrowing should be through government development bonds.

On government spending he said: "On one hand spending should not increase in a way leading to accumulation of debts on the government and hence increase the burdens of servicing these debts. On the other, government spending should not be slow in a way that would negatively affect economic activity."
He said "government spending in general is to support the private sector", which, under the government development plan "carries the biggest burden of economic development".

The payment of 22 billion riyals in arrears to farmers and contractors had restored confidence to the private sector, Asaf said. "There are some steps being discussed and...will be adopted that will give another boost to this important sector."
